'''Thomas William Hungerford''' (March 21, 1936 – November 28, 2014)<ref name=obit>{{Cite web|url=https://www.colliersfuneralhome.com/obituary/6294507?lud=D173D71D865564DA6D19E9F951B6DFE6|title=Obituary for Thomas W. Hungerford|publisher=Collier's Funeral Home}}</ref> was an American mathematician who worked in [[algebra]] and [[mathematics education]]. He is the author or coauthor of several widely used<ref>[http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/264515.Algebra Algebra] ([[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]) at [[goodreads]]</ref> and widely cited<ref>[http://docjax.net/g/search?q=thomas+w.+hungerford&x=8&y=10  Citations at docjax.net the document search engine]</ref> textbooks covering high-school to graduate-level mathematics. From 1963 until 1980, he taught at the [[University of Washington]] and then at [[Cleveland State University]] until 2003. From 2003–2014 he was at [[Saint Louis University (United States)|Saint Louis University]]. Hungerford had a special interest in promoting the use of technology to teach mathematics.

== Early life and education ==
Hungerford was born in [[Oak Park, Illinois]], in 1936. At age 16, he moved to [[St. Louis|St. Louis, Missouri]], where he attended [[St. Louis University High School]] and graduated as the valedictorian of his high school class.<ref name="obit" />

After high school, Hungerford enrolled at the [[College of the Holy Cross]] in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in mathematics in 1958.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=1958 |title=The Class of 1958: Seniors |url=https://crossworks.holycross.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?filename=4&article=1033&context=purple_patcher&type=additional |access-date=17 May 2026 |website=Purple Patcher |publisher=[[College of the Holy Cross]] |page=77}}</ref> As an undergraduate at Holy Cross, he wrote a senior thesis on [[topological space]].<ref name=":0" /> He then pursued graduate studies at the [[University of Chicago]], where he earned his [[Ph.D.]] in mathematics in 1963 under the supervision of mathematician [[Saunders Mac Lane]].<ref name="obit" /> His doctoral dissertation was titled, "Bockstein spectra".<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 14, 1963 |title=Bockstein Spectra |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/4ec89f3065eb757522d2b1bfeb970f7c/1?cbl=18750&diss=y&pq-origsite=gscholar |access-date=19 May 2026 |publisher=[[Proquest]] |type=PhD Thesis}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
After receiving his doctorate in 1963, Hungerford began teaching mathematics at the [[University of Washington]] in Seattle, where he remained until 1980.<ref name="Collier">{{cite web |title=Thomas W. Hungerford Obituary |url=https://www.colliersfuneralhome.com/obituaries/thomas-hungerford |access-date=September 17, 2026 |website=Collier's Funeral Home}}</ref> During his years at Washington, he published research on subjects including Bockstein spectra, hyperhomology, multilinear maps, and the structure of principal ideal rings.<ref name="CJM1968">{{cite journal |last=Hungerford |first=Thomas W. |year=1968 |title=A Characterization of the Hyperhomology Groups of the Tensor Product |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-of-mathematics/article/characterization-of-the-hyperhomology-groups-of-the-tensor-product/AB538B590525FAA5B2DE282D6288CE66 |journal=[[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=20 |pages=505–510 |doi=10.4153/CJM-1968-049-x |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref><ref name="Multi1966">{{cite journal |last=Hungerford |first=Thomas William |year=1966 |title=A description of Multi (A1, · · · , An) by generators and relations |url=https://msp.org/pjm/1966/16-1/pjm-v16-n1-p06-p.pdf |journal=[[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=61–76 |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref> In a 1968 paper in the ''Pacific Journal of Mathematics'', he proved that every principal ideal ring is a finite direct sum of rings, each of which is a homomorphic image of a principal ideal domain.<ref name="PJM1968">{{cite journal |last=Hungerford |first=Thomas W. |year=1968 |title=On the structure of principal ideal rings |url=https://msp.org/pjm/1968/25-3/pjm-v25-n3-p11-p.pdf |journal=[[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=543–547 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1968.25.543 |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref>

Hungerford's graduate-level textbook ''Algebra'' was originally published by [[Holt, Rinehart and Winston]] in 1974 and was subsequently issued by [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] as volume 73 of its ''[[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]'' series.<ref name="SpringerAlgebra">{{cite web |title=Algebra |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4612-6101-8 |access-date=September 17, 2026 |publisher=[[Springer Nature]]}}</ref> The book covers groups, rings, modules, fields and Galois theory, linear algebra, commutative rings and modules, ring structure, and category theory.<ref name="SpringerAlgebra" /> In 1980, Hungerford moved from Washington to [[Cleveland State University]], where he taught mathematics until 2001.<ref name="Collier" /> 

In addition to his research in algebra, Hungerford published work in mathematics education and authored or coauthored more than a dozen mathematics textbooks from the high-school level to graduate level.<ref name="PearsonBio">{{cite book |last1=Lial |first1=Margaret L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MrzGEAAAQBAJ |title=Mathematics with Applications in the Management, Natural and Social Sciences |last2=Hungerford |first2=Thomas W. |last3=Holcomb |first3=John P. |last4=Mullins |first4=Bernadette |publisher=Pearson Higher Ed |year=2023 |edition=13th |access-date=September 17, 2026 |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> He promoted the use of technology in mathematics instruction, served as a referee and reviewer for mathematical journals, and participated on [[National Science Foundation]] panels that evaluated grant applications.<ref name="PearsonBio" /> After returning to St. Louis in 2003, Hungerford maintained an office at [[Saint Louis University]] until 2013, when he retired from writing and revising textbooks.<ref name="Collier" /> His later textbooks included works in abstract algebra, precalculus, college algebra, trigonometry, finite mathematics, and applied mathematics.<ref name="PearsonBio" />
